idiom_name: Callable[[T], bool] with TypeGuard / TypeIs type predicates
implementation_notes: Validators are plain callables (Callable[[T], bool], or Callable[[T], list[str]] for reasons), and the standard library supplies the narrowing half of the pattern: typing.TypeGuard[T] (3.10) and typing.TypeIs[T] (3.13) mark a boolean-returning function as a static type predicate, so after the if the type checker treats the value as narrowed - the Predicate idea with the proof carried to the caller. contramap is a composed callable or lambda over a projection, divide is all(...)/functools.reduce over a rule tuple (use a list comprehension rather than all when every failure must be reported), and choose is match over a class hierarchy or a dataclass/Enum variant.
code_sketch:
from typing import TypeIs

def is_port(v: object) -> TypeIs[int]:            # narrows int | str to int
    return isinstance(v, int) and 0 < v < 65536

RULES: tuple[Callable[[Config], str | None], ...] = (check_host, check_port)

def validate(cfg: Config) -> list[str]:
    return [msg for rule in RULES if (msg := rule(cfg)) is not None]   # keep all failures
pitfalls: A TypeGuard/TypeIs annotation is a claim, not a check: the function body must still perform the runtime test, and TypeGuard (unlike TypeIs) is unsound when the caller needs narrowing in both branches.
all()/any() short-circuit, so a rule list built with them reports only the first failure - collect verdicts in a list when the caller must display every error.
Closures over mutable state (a config dict, a rule list mutated later) silently change what a validator means; build rule sets at import time from immutable data.

variants.name: Pydantic v2 Annotated validators (declarative, accumulating)
variants.idiom_name: Annotated[T, AfterValidator(f)] / field_validator; ValidationError with loc paths
variants.implementation_notes: Pydantic v2 carries the rule in the type: Annotated[int, AfterValidator(is_port)] makes every use of that annotated type validated, field_validator attaches reusable checks to a field, and model_validator handles cross-field rules with the already-resolved values. Failures raise a ValidationError listing every issue with its loc path - the accumulating verdict, for free. Choose it when data arrives as JSON or config, or when the same rules must also drive serialization and OpenAPI output; prefer the plain-callable variant for in-process checks that never touch a model.
pitfalls: An AfterValidator runs on the parsed value and its return value becomes the value: keep validators type-preserving and raise ValueError/AssertionError to reject, because a silent transformation widens the annotated type.
Model validators see only the fields that already validated, in definition order, so cross-field rules must tolerate missing data (ValidationInfo.data).
Constraint order is fixed (before/after parsing): a rule that must inspect the raw input has to be a BeforeValidator, not an AfterValidator with defensive parsing.
